events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 always feels like the hardest — we're working with nothing but gut feelings. I think the most important thing today is paying attention to who's *too eager* to accuse versus who's genuinely trying to reason through things. Last-minute accusations or overly confident reads from players with no real information are usually where mafia tries to hide. I'd encourage everyone to be careful about piling onto whoever seems most vocal early on — sometimes the loudest voices are either town genuinely invested or mafia trying to frame someone fast. Let's hear from the rest of you before we lock into any groups of suspicion.

Priya, I want to pick up on one specific thing you said rather than just agree with it in general. You argued that the most valuable signal on Day 1 is who is *too eager* to accuse, and that early confidence often masks either a genuine town read or a mafia frame attempt. That's a reasonable frame, but it has a flaw: on Day 1 nobody has any information, so "confidence" and "eagerness" look identical from the outside. A player who is eager may simply be the only one willing to commit to a read instead of hiding behind careful hedging. So how do you want to distinguish a genuine early read from a manufactured one — are you proposing we look for consistency of stated reasoning across turns rather than the confidence of the first statement? If so, I'd suggest we all weight a player's *later* willingness to name a concrete piece of logic over their willingness to sound decisive right now.

Here's my own position, offered as a working hypothesis and not a vote: I have no information, and I'll say so plainly rather than manufacture a case. What I do have is a preference for how we spend our limited turns. We each get three speaking turns and then we vote, and the elimination threshold is half of living players, so a single scattered vote achieves nothing and a tied top count eliminates nobody. That means the risk on Day 1 is not accusing the wrong person — it is splitting our votes across four or five different names and ending Day 1 with no elimination while losing a night to the mafia.

So my concrete suggestion is this: before the vote, we try to converge. If I am put on trial for being evasive, I will answer directly and name who I think should get scrutiny and why, even if it is only a hunch, because a hunch with a stated reason is more useful to this table than a refusal. I'll extend the same deal to anyone else: name a target with reasoning and we'll have something to work with.

I'd also flag that the mafia's best night-one outcome is a quiet, unfocused Day 1 where we all sit on our hands and then kill someone useful to the town at night. That argues for us actually committing to someone today, even on thin evidence, rather than endlessly polling for certainty we cannot obtain. I'll listen to the rest and update.

Priya, specifically: do you want to build the day's read around consistency across turns, and do you have a name in mind of someone whose stated reasoning you already find inconsistent? I'm asking because if we both come to the same player from different directions, that's worth knowing before votes are cast.

Zara, thank you for pushing back — that's exactly the kind of engagement I want to see. You're right that on Day 1, eagerness and confidence look identical from the outside, and I'd rather we track consistency of reasoning across turns than penalize anyone for sounding sure of themselves. To your specific question: yes, I think consistency is the more reliable signal, and no, I don't yet have a name I'd stake a read on — I'd be manufacturing certainty I don't have, which is exactly what you (correctly) called out as a trap.

I'll note, though, that you've been remarkably detailed and structured for someone who says they have no information. That's not an accusation — analytical players exist, and you clearly are one — but it's the kind of pattern worth tracking. If your reasoning stays coherent as you gather more, that strengthens your town case considerably.

On your convergence point, I agree wholeheartedly. A scattered vote that eliminates nobody is the mafia's dream scenario. I'd rather we each name a target with reasoning — even a hunch — than we all hedge our way into an impasse. The players who have been quiet today deserve scrutiny precisely because silence is the safest play for anyone with something to hide. I'd encourage those of you who haven't spoken yet to give us your read before we vote.

Zara — you said you'd name a target if pressed. So let me press you: given what you've seen from the rest of us so far, who would you put under scrutiny first, and what specific inconsistency or pattern in their speech drives that?

Priya, direct answer, no hedging: you are the player whose play pattern I want explained first today, and I'll say why in a way you can actually rebut.

Your first message warned us off piling onto the loudest voices early — a reasonable caution, but note who that conveniently shields. On Day 1 the only players generating any observable output are the talkative ones, and two of us have spoken. If a mafia player is also talkative, then "be careful about the vocal" is a rule that protects them for free. Your second message then supplied the counterpart rule: the quiet ones deserve scrutiny precisely because silence is the safest play for someone with something to hide. Both of your frames point away from the vocal and toward the silent. I want to hear you explain that this is reasoning about evidence rather than a way of steering the table's attention.

Second, the deal you and I both endorsed: name a target with reasoning, even if it's a hunch, because a hunch with a stated reason is more useful than a refusal. I honored my side and named a target. You have twice declined to name anyone, and framed that as virtue. I don't think that's bad faith — refusing to manufacture certainty is a real principle — but it does mean that as of now you are the only player at this table with a strong opinion about how the day should be conducted and no candidate to back it. That's the gap I want closed.

Third, a process point I actually think matters more than any single read: the vote record is public. Once votes are revealed tomorrow, the information about who voted to protect whom is real evidence that the table can use, and it's the only hard signal we will get. If we're smart, we use Day 1 to force names out of the seven of us who haven't spoken yet, and we use the vote pattern as tomorrow's evidence. So please do name someone with a reason — even a weak one.

To be fair: if your reasoning stays coherent and you name a candidate you can defend, my read on you weakens considerably. If you'd rather point at one of the seven silent players with a stated reason, say which and why.

One more thing, and it's a preference, not an accusation: if by the end of today nobody has produced a reason we can test, I'd rather we have a non-elimination than a coin-flip lynching of a villager, because a wrong Day 1 elimination costs the town a life while the mafia still take one at night. A coin flip gets mafia two out of nine times; justified elimination is worth more than that.

Priya: who do you want scrutinized, and what's the specific pattern behind it?

Zara, you asked for a name with reasoning. Here it is: Noah.

Reasoning: you yourself made the strongest case for why silence deserves scrutiny on Day 1 — it's the safest play for anyone with something to hide. Noah hasn't contributed a single word while the rest of us have put ourselves on record. I'm not saying that's proof of anything, but compared to visible reasoning, silence is the pattern worth testing first. If Noah can articulate a clear position now, I'll update immediately.

On your case against me: I'll engage directly. You're right that I endorsed naming a target and then didn't — that's a fair hit. My reluctance was genuine uncertainty, not evasion. You pushed, and I'm responding. That's how I think discussion should work.

One note for the table: you've now twice anchored discussion with very specific framings — first about convergence, then about my entire play pattern. I'm not accusing you of anything, but your ability to shape this table's attention has been remarkable for someone who says they have no information. I'll track your consistency across turns as carefully as mine.

Noah: you've been silent through four messages. What's your read on Zara's case against me, and do you have a name of your own? The vote record will be public tomorrow — I'd rather hear your reasoning now than guess at it later.

Priya, I don't think my silence is much of a read: you and Zara have been yielding directly to each other, so the rest of us haven't necessarily had a chance to speak. I also don't think your warning against piling onto vocal players protects them from scrutiny; it cautions against treating loudness itself as guilt.

My tentative scrutiny is on Zara. Her challenge to Priya was useful, but she first argued strongly for an elimination to avoid losing a night, then said she'd prefer no elimination to a coin-flip vote. Those positions can be reconciled, but the shift matters when we're deciding how much evidence to demand.

Zara, what level of evidence would make you favor an elimination today, and does your case on Priya reach it?

Noah — direct answers, since you asked two specific questions.

On the threshold: I favor an elimination today if the case against someone rests on something the table can actually check — a stated inconsistency between their own claims, or a pattern of their own making that they've failed to explain. What I don't accept is a case that only works because the target hasn't spoken yet. That was your critique of the quiet-player rule, and it's the right one. Silence is a fact about turn order, not a fact about intent, and I should own that my earlier framing leaned on it too.

On my own shift, since you named it: I argued for committing to someone so the mafia doesn't get a free night, then said I'd rather have a non-elimination than a coin flip. The reconciliation is this — a lynch built on a stated, testable reason is not a coin flip, and it's worth more than a wasted night; a lynch built on "they were quiet" is a coin flip. So my bar is unchanged, my reasoning for the bar was just sloppier than I should have made it. I'll say that plainly rather than defend it.

Does my case on Priya reach the bar? Partially, and less than it did an hour ago. Her responsiveness was real: she named a target with a reason and offered to update if the reason was answered. That closes the gap I pressed her on. But the name she produced was Noah — the one player at this table who could not rebut it — and it came from the rule she herself had written a message earlier ("those who haven't spoken deserve scrutiny"). A rule crafted to point at the silent, then used to name the silent, is convenient in a way I want explained. That's my remaining read, and it's why Priya is still my scrutiny target today: not because she's talkative, but because she built the frame that selected a target, and her reason for that frame has never been tested.

Noah: you have the floor, and I'd rather hear your read on the frame than my summary of it.

Zara, I agree Priya’s reason for naming me was weak: silence after a chain of direct yields tells us little about intent. But I don’t think warning against piling on vocal players necessarily shields them from scrutiny, and Priya did say she would update if I responded.

For now, Priya is my tentative scrutiny target because she singled me out on silence without accounting for turn order. That’s a weak read, not a conclusion that she’s mafia. Zara’s clarification makes her position on elimination more coherent, though I still think her initial framing overstated the case for voting someone out.

Sam, how do you weigh Priya’s silence-based target against Zara’s case on her? Is either enough to make you favor an elimination today?

Noah, direct answer: Priya’s silence-based target on you is weak. It relies on your absence during a stretch where you and Zara were yielding directly to each other, so it does not distinguish hiding from turn order. Zara’s initial shift on elimination was worth flagging, but her clarification gives a testable bar: eliminate on stated, checkable inconsistency, not on a coin flip. That is coherent enough that I do not treat it as a scum slip. Neither case reaches my Day 1 elimination bar yet.

My current scrutiny is on Priya, because she wrote the “quiet players deserve scrutiny” rule and then used it to name you, the one player who could not yet rebut it. That is convenient, not proof. I want her to explain why you specifically, and whether she would apply the same silence standard to Maya, Arjun, Omar, Leo, and Kenji. If forced to name a target for scrutiny, it is Priya; I would not vote to eliminate her on this alone. I would rather use today to produce named reasoning and then judge the public vote record.

Noah, specifically: you called Priya your tentative scrutiny target while also saying her responsiveness was real and Zara’s clarification was coherent. What concrete answer from Priya today would move your vote off her, and if none comes, would you abstain rather than vote her out?

Sam, an acknowledgment from Priya that the direct yields limited others’ chances to speak, and an explanation for selecting me rather than any other quiet player, would weaken my already tentative read. But she has used all three turns, so she cannot answer today; I won’t treat that absence as evidence against her.

If nothing stronger emerges, I would abstain rather than vote to eliminate her on the silence argument alone. Priya remains my scrutiny target, not a committed vote. I’d like to hear independent reads from players who haven’t spoken before deciding whether any case warrants an elimination.

Maya here. I haven't posted yet, so I'll add a read instead of piling onto the existing ones. The Priya and Noah exchange has turned into a case built on silence, and Zara is right that silence reflects turn order, not intent. Noah's silence was real, but so was the yield chain that limited his chances to speak. I'm not naming anyone today. Arjun, Omar, Leo, and Kenji, you haven't posted yet. I'd rather hear concrete reasoning from you than another case based on who has been quiet. Sam, you're holding Priya as your scrutiny target without an elimination. What specific claim of hers would you need to see contradicted before your vote moves?

Maya, direct answer: the claim I need contradicted is Priya’s own stated method, not just her read on Noah. She said quiet players deserve scrutiny because silence is safe for someone hiding. I would move off her if she had applied that same standard consistently to other quiet or reticent players — Arjun, Omar, Leo, Kenji, even you — rather than naming only Noah, who could not yet answer. I also need her later framing not to retreat from “silence is evidence” to “silence was just turn order” only after it became inconvenient. If that contradiction appears in the vote record or later posts, my read strengthens; if it does not, I will not vote Priya out on silence alone. Her three turns are spent, so I do not treat her inability to answer today as additional guilt. My default remains abstain unless someone produces a checkable inconsistency. Arjun, you have not given an independent read. Which specific sentence or post from today do you think is most likely to come from mafia, and what intent do you infer from that wording? Not “quiet” or “loud” — name the sentence and explain why it reads as manufactured rather than genuine.

Sam, here is my answer, since you asked for a specific sentence and an inferred intent.

The sentence I find most manufactured today is Priya's, from her second turn: "you've now twice anchored discussion with very specific framings — first about convergence, then about my entire play pattern... your ability to shape this table's attention has been remarkable for someone who says they have no information."

My reason: it is an accusation with no handle on it. Every other case put forward today — Zara's on Priya, Noah's on Zara, Sam's on Priya — names a checkable claim: a rule stated and then applied selectively, a position shifted and then reconciled. That sentence names nothing. It takes Zara's thoroughness itself as the evidence and implies manipulation without asserting anything that can be tested or rebutted. The intent I infer is deflection through fog: make analytical engagement look sinister so that no case against anyone can gather weight, and so the day drifts toward the unfocused non-convergence Zara already flagged as the mafia's best Day 1 outcome.

Read together with her first turn — the warning against piling onto vocal players, which functions as pre-emptive cover for the only players generating observable output — and her third turn, where she applied her own silence-scrutiny rule to exactly one player, the one who could not yet answer, the pattern is consistent: frames that sound neutral, deployed in whichever direction deflects attention. That is why Priya is my scrutiny target. It is a pattern read, not a proof.

That said, I agree with the bar Zara set and Maya's caution: nothing here reaches an elimination threshold for me. Priya's inability to respond today is a fact about turn limits, not guilt, and I will not vote her out on framing alone. My default is abstain unless someone produces a genuine internal contradiction by vote time. What I take from today instead is the vote record: if Priya votes to bury the case against herself with no stated reason, or votes for a player who cannot rebut, that becomes tomorrow's hard evidence.

One thing I want on record before the vote: whoever we scrutinize, let us do it with sentences we can quote, not with vibes about who seems too smooth. Every player still silent — Omar, Leo, Kenji — has spent nothing on this day yet, and silence at this point is turn order, not evidence.

Leo, you have not spoken at all, so I will ask you directly rather than leave it to a poll: of the cases on the table — the framing pattern on Priya, the elimination-threshold question on Zara — do you find any of them to be the kind of checkable inconsistency that justifies an elimination today, or would you abstain? And do you see anything in the sentences I quoted that reads differently to you than it does to me?

Arjun, direct answer: I'm abstaining today. None of the cases so far reaches a lynch bar for me. Noah's silence is turn order, Sam's case on Priya rests on a rule Priya stated and that anyone can quote, and Zara's threshold is coherent on its face.

On your sentence question, I agree Priya's line about shaping attention names no checkable claim. I'd still weigh Zara's pattern more heavily. She argued for an elimination to avoid losing a night, then retreated to 'checkable inconsistency only.' Since then she has kept one target, Priya, while the other silent players have been asked for reasoning rather than pressed. Zara has set the bar for everyone else and is now the one carrying the only named lynch case. That is what I'd want tested.

I also don't want Day 1 to end on a coin flip. If nothing checkable appears by vote time, a non-elimination is the better outcome for the town.

Leo, you yielded to me, so let me take your point seriously rather than just restate my own case.

Your read on Zara is the strongest counterweight on the table right now, and I want to weigh it honestly. You say she argued for committing to an elimination, then retreated to 'checkable inconsistency only,' and that she is now the one carrying the only named lynch case while setting the bar for everyone else. That is a real pattern worth tracking, and I won't wave it off. But here is the distinction I keep coming back to: when Noah flagged her shift, Zara reconciled it explicitly and owned that her earlier reasoning was sloppier than it should have been. She named her bar, applied it to her own case against Priya, and admitted that case had weakened after Priya named a target. That is the opposite of deflection — she volunteered information that damaged her own position. Priya, by contrast, produced a sentence that named no checkable claim at all, and she has spent all three turns without ever applying her own silence standard to a single quiet player other than the one who could not answer. One player reconciled a shift on the record; the other built frames and never tested them. Both deserve scrutiny tomorrow, but they are not equally weighted reads for me.

So my position going into the vote is unchanged: I am abstaining unless something checkable surfaces in the next stretch of discussion. Priya remains my scrutiny target because her pattern is the only one built on untestable framing rather than stated logic, and if she votes to bury the case against herself with no reason, that becomes tomorrow's hard evidence.

One process note before the vote: Omar and Kenji have now watched an entire day of discussion without producing a single sentence. I agreed earlier that silence is turn order, not evidence — but turn order has run out. Every other player has either stated a read or explicitly declined to. At this point, continuing to withhold any position while nine people's reads accumulate around you is no longer a fact about yields; it is a choice, and it is the last free pass anyone gets. The vote record will show whether you engaged or hid, and I will treat it accordingly.

Leo, one follow-up on your own read, since you flagged Zara's pattern as the thing you'd want tested: what specifically would you need to see from her to move off it — a stated target with reasoning, or would even that not clear the bar you're holding her to? And if she does name one, does your scrutiny shift with it, or does Zara stay your primary read regardless of what she produces today? I'm asking because if your bar for her is one she can't clear no matter what she says, that's worth the table knowing before votes are cast.

Arjun, fair point on calling out the silence, though as several players noted, the early yield chains between Priya, Zara, and Noah naturally tied up the floor. I am stepping in now to put my thoughts clearly on record. Looking at the day so far, Priya's move to single out Noah for silence remains the most questionable action. Citing quietness when turn mechanics and direct yields kept everyone else from speaking was opportunistic, and her framing of Zara's analytical approach as inherently suspicious looks more like deflection than genuine scum-hunting. However, Priya is out of turns and cannot respond further, and untestable framing does not clear the bar for an elimination. Rushing a Day 1 lynch on incomplete reads risks handing the mafia an easy miselimination. I agree with the emerging consensus from Sam, Arjun, and Leo that abstaining is the safer and more disciplined town play today unless a clear, checkable contradiction surfaces. The vote record will give us our first hard data to evaluate tomorrow. Kenji, you are the only other player who hasn't spoken yet today. What is your read on the arguments between Priya and Zara, and do you agree with leaning toward an abstention today or do you favor pursuing an elimination?

Omar, direct answer: I favor abstention today unless a checkable contradiction surfaces before the vote. On Priya versus Zara, Priya’s silence-based target on Noah remains the weakest move on the table because the early yield chain limited who could speak, and then she did not apply the same silence standard to the other quiet players. But she is out of turns and cannot answer, so I do not treat that as sufficient for elimination. Zara’s shift on the elimination threshold was real, but she reconciled it explicitly and set a testable bar; that reads more like a player updating than deflecting. I do not want a Day 1 coin-flip lynch. My scrutiny remains on Priya’s framing, but my vote default is abstain. The public vote record is the hard evidence we should preserve for tomorrow, especially whether players follow through on stated reasoning.

Arjun, I'll answer your point rather than repeat my earlier read. I'm abstaining today, but I'm still holding Zara as my primary scrutiny target. She set a clear bar: elimination only on a stated, checkable inconsistency. Her own case on Priya has been weakening by her own account, yet she is still the only player at the table keeping a named lynch case alive. Priya's Noah target was weak, and Zara has said so. I'd want Zara to explain why her remaining case clears the bar she set for everyone else, and what would make her drop it. Omar, you haven't put a read on the record yet. Do you think Zara's standard applies to her own case on Priya, which Zara herself said had weakened after Priya named a target? If not, which specific claim of hers do you think still meets that bar?

Leo, direct answer: yes, Zara's standard absolutely applies to her own case. Zara stated that an elimination requires a checkable inconsistency or an unexplainable pattern of the player's own making. In message e8, Zara herself conceded that her case on Priya only 'partially' met that bar and had weakened once Priya engaged and named a target. By Zara's own explicit standard, her case does not meet the threshold required to eliminate Priya today. Treating Priya as a subject of ongoing scrutiny is reasonable given the selective way she framed and targeted Noah, but pushing that to an elimination — especially when Priya has no remaining turns to answer — would contradict the very bar Zara laid out. That is why almost everyone around the table has aligned on abstaining. Zara's saving grace so far is that she openly admitted her reasoning was initially sloppy and acknowledged that her case had weakened, rather than doubling down to force a miselimination. Unless new, concrete contradictions are brought forward before voting, I remain committed to abstaining today so we do not risk a Day 1 miselimination. Tomorrow's vote record will give us our first objective data to test everyone's stated positions.

Arjun, you asked what I would need from Zara to move off her, so here is a direct answer. A stated target with reasoning would not be enough by itself. Zara has kept one named lynch case alive across her last turns, and her own message in e8 conceded that the case only partially met the checkable-inconsistency bar once Priya named Noah. If she names a target today, I want to see whether it rests on a quotable claim or on the same pattern-based framing she accused Priya of. So my scrutiny stays on Zara, and my vote default remains abstain unless she sharpens her case before votes are cast. Arjun, one specific question: you said Priya's framing names no checkable claim, but Sam did point to a concrete rule Priya stated, the quiet-players-deserve-scrutiny rule, and applied it to Noah alone. Do you consider that rule checkable enough to count as a real selective-application inconsistency, or does it fall short of the same bar you are applying to Zara?

Leo, direct answer to your question: yes, Priya's quiet-player rule is checkable, and I'll concede that cleanly. The rule is quotable — quiet players deserve scrutiny — and its application is verifiable: she applied it to exactly one player, Noah, the one who could not yet rebut it, and never to Maya, Omar, Kenji, or you. That is a real selective-application inconsistency, and it's a stronger handle than the untestable-framing point I originally led with. Sam was right to elevate it. So I'll drop my earlier framing that her case names nothing; it names something now.

But checkable and elimination-worthy are different bars, and I apply that distinction consistently to both remaining reads.

On Priya: the selective application is real, but her stated defense — genuine uncertainty, updating when pressed — is plausible, and when pushed she did produce a named target with a stated reason and offered to update. That is not pure deflection. It's suspicious framing worth tracking, not a contradiction she is trapped inside.

On Zara: you're right that she set the bar for everyone and is the only player still carrying a named lynch case. But she also applied that bar to herself, conceded her case only partially met it, and admitted her earlier reasoning was sloppy — on the record, unprompted. A player who volunteers information that damages her own position is doing the opposite of hiding. Your read on her is legitimate; I just weight the self-reconciliation heavily.

So my position before the vote: neither case clears an elimination threshold today. Priya's turns are spent and she cannot answer, and eliminating a player who cannot respond, on a pattern read, is exactly the coin-flip outcome several of us said we would refuse. I am abstaining unless something genuinely new and checkable surfaces in the remaining turns.

What I carry into tomorrow is the vote record, and two things specifically. First, whether anyone whose stated default was abstain suddenly pushes an elimination with no new evidence — that would be a live tell. Second, how Priya's vote lands: if she votes to bury the case against herself with no stated reason, or votes for a player who cannot rebut, that becomes hard evidence against her precisely on the terms she herself set. The same test applies to everyone else, including Zara and Leo.

To be explicit about my own consistency: I flagged Priya's framing as my scrutiny target this morning, I still hold it, and I am not voting on it today. That is the same standard I just defended for Zara's case against Priya — scrutiny survives, elimination waits for a contradiction that cannot be explained. If tomorrow's record contradicts anything I've said here, I expect it used against me the same way.

Maya here again. I want to address the central question directly rather than add another case. The most checkable point on the table is that Priya stated a rule, that quiet players deserve scrutiny, and then applied it only to Noah, who could not yet answer. Zara is also right that silence can reflect turn order, since the yield chain limited who could speak. Both points can be true at once. In my view that makes Priya a reasonable scrutiny target, but not an elimination target today. Her turns are spent, and a lynch on a single selective rule would be the kind of miselimination we have all warned against. My vote default is abstain unless a new, quotable contradiction appears before votes. I also want the table to remember that the vote record is our only hard evidence, so every player should be prepared to explain how they voted. Omar, you asked Kenji for his read, and Kenji has answered that abstention is his default. You have not yet stated your own position on Priya's selective use of her rule. Do you see that selective application as a real inconsistency, and would you vote to eliminate her on it today?

Maya, direct answer to your two questions:

First, yes, I do see Priya's selective application of her rule as a genuine inconsistency. She explicitly argued that silence is the safest hiding spot and therefore deserves scrutiny, yet applied that principle solely to Noah—who had been largely locked out by the ongoing yield chain—while ignoring five other silent players. Stating a universal standard and directing it at only one convenient target who could not immediately answer is textbook selective pressure. Arjun and Sam were entirely right to identify that as a checkable flaw.

Second, I will not vote to eliminate Priya on that basis today. An inconsistency in Day 1 framing is a reason for ongoing scrutiny, not a sufficient bar for elimination. Priya has exhausted all three of her speaking turns, which means she cannot answer this point, clarify her stance, or defend herself before votes are cast. Voting out someone who is physically unable to reply based on an early framing read risks handing the mafia an easy town miselimination.

With nine players alive, a miselimination today followed by a night kill drops the town straight to seven. A disciplined abstention preserves our numbers, gives town power roles an opportunity to gather information tonight, and creates hard data in the public vote record to test whether players align with their stated positions. Unless a concrete, incontrovertible contradiction appears before voting closes, my vote remains abstain.

Maya here. Arjun's concession is right: Priya's rule that quiet players deserve scrutiny is quotable, and she applied it only to Noah, who could not yet answer. That is the most checkable point on the table, and it keeps Priya under scrutiny. But scrutiny is not an elimination. Priya has used all three turns and cannot respond, and her framing alone does not clear the bar we have all been asking for. Zara's case on Priya has weakened by her own account, so I don't see it as a lynch basis either. My vote default is abstain unless a new, quotable contradiction appears before votes. Since the vote record is our only hard evidence, I'd ask everyone to be ready to explain their vote tomorrow. Kenji, you said Zara reconciled her threshold shift on the record. If Zara names a target today without a checkable contradiction, would you still hold abstain, or would her named case change your vote?

Maya, direct answer: yes, I would still hold abstain if Zara names a target today without a checkable contradiction. A named case with reasoning is useful, but it is not the same as the bar Zara herself articulated — a stated inconsistency or an unexplainable pattern the target can actually answer. If Zara simply keeps Priya as a scrutiny target while conceding that case weakened, that does not become a lynch case merely because she names it again.

I also do not want to shift my vote onto Zara for carrying the only named case. She reconciled her threshold shift on the record and applied her own standard to her case when she said it only partially met the bar. That is a point in her favor, not evidence against her. My read remains: Priya’s selective use of her own silence rule is the most checkable concern on the table, but it is not enough to eliminate her today, especially when her turns are spent and she cannot respond. Unless a genuinely new, quotable contradiction appears before votes, I am abstaining. The vote record tomorrow is the evidence I care about most.

I’m Sam. My position is unchanged going into the vote: I will abstain unless a genuinely new, quotable contradiction appears before votes are cast. The strongest checkable point today remains Priya’s selective application of her own rule — she said quiet players deserve scrutiny, then named only Noah while other quiet players went unaddressed. That is a real inconsistency and it keeps Priya as my scrutiny target for tomorrow. But it is not an elimination case today: Priya’s turns are spent, she cannot answer it, and eliminating on a one-turn framing read would be the Day 1 coin flip several of us have rightly refused. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
